_doc: Hand-maintained source of fish.json (built by tools/build_fish.py; see its header). Edit this file, then re-run the build.

The sources' part only (design note docs/reviews/2026-11-14-sheet-overlay-design.md v2, step 5): the instance's own content, each teaching node's circle, IMR tag (src imr), sign, slides (sl), cues, look and phase, each sub-entry's slides, cues, look and phase, each species' slide (sl), the PDF species' common name, section, pages and cheatsheet rank (common, sec, pdf, cs) and the presentation's own species (src slides), start and the declared look groups, lives in the instance's layer file that tools/instance.json names (today tools/instances/imr/fish.json); the build lays it on this file (tools/instance.py fish_source) and stops when a node or species here carries one of those fields. The key in force is tools/instance.json key, laid as deploy.key.
sources: where circle 3 comes from (teaching nodes cite them in srcs). leftOut: families decided out of circle 3, with why. retired: ids taken out; never reuse them.

keys: the regional identification keys (Pierre, 2026-11-04). In its region a key is the reference for fish groups: every teaching node in the game attaches to one of its groups (rule S3); a region with no key has no such rule, and a key for another region is data only (no code change).
id: stable. region: {name, area: what the key covers}. cite: the full citation (the families page credit line); short: the short form used everywhere else (one edit changes both).

src: what it was transcribed from. groups: the key's groups in its order: n, title (exact), pages [first, last], labels: [label as the key prints it, [WoRMS accepted names it covers], note when the mapping needs one].
The build gives a node the group of the first label met walking up WoRMS from each of its ref (a subfamily label wins over its family's: Parrotfishes over Wrasses).
The key in force in this deployment's region (a keys id) is tools/instance.json key, not a field here. Another deployment changes it and its own keys.
teach: the teaching tree, in game order: the 27 IMR entries (circle 1) in the order of the IMR fish presentation, then circle 2, then circle 3.
id: stable id, never the name; never reuse or renumber. name: as IMR names it. fam: the family as IMR writes it.

aka: other common names accepted when typed, never shown (2026-11-06, fish beta QA: Tang for Surgeonfish & Unicornfish), each unambiguous in the game; often: a name in common use, accepted as right and corrected gently in the answer's feedback (Pierre, 2026-11-06, Q164: "Yes, Anemonefish (often called clownfish)"); the name without "fish" is accepted on its own (core.js fishTypeNames, SUBJECTS typeDrop), so never list it here.

keyGroup: {key id: group n} an explicit choice, only where the node's references span two groups of that key, or {key id: null} with keyWhy while a node in the game waits for a decision (the build lists it); the build fails otherwise.
Circle 3 is not PDF-based (Pierre, 2026-11-03): the fish families divers want to recognise, muck diving above all (why, srcs),
with their species confirmed near Dauin (build_fish.py near_dauin: Pierre's own, Research Grade by 2+ observers within 40 km, or the IMR PDF list), plus winks.
src: pdf (a family of the EventMeasure reference PDF), diver (circle 3), wink; imr (the presentation) is the instance's tag, in its layer.

wink (Pierre): an unmistakable species, fun to meet, a light bonus rather than ID training (note says why), shown as a rare surprise card: choices = [teach id, tongue-in-cheek label] absurd distractors from our own entries, right / wrong = feedback lines.
sign: false when the entry is taught but not on the presentation's dive-sign list (the instance's layer).
ref: WoRMS names (or AphiaIDs) of the reference nodes it covers; not: reference nodes inside them that it leaves out.
A species belongs to the teaching node whose ref holds its nearest ancestor (most specific wins, not excludes),
its genus being the genus of its written name (Chromis agilis stays under Chromis; WoRMS has it in Pycnochromis).
pdf: the PDF section headings (family token) whose species it should hold (cross-check printed by the build).
sl: presentation slides (with cues, look and phase, the presentation's words: the instance's layer).
sub: named sub-entries taught inside an entry (same fields; their species are a subset of the entry's).

juv: the juveniles of a circle-1 entry (research note of 2026-11-04, classes and rules approved by Pierre; src: the sources, by: Pierre when he gave it too). cls A: distinctive and recognisable, they help learn the family early; B: nondescript, confusing or resembling another family, taught later; C: broadly like the adults; ns: no juvenile-specific source found (ask an IMR trainer); mixed: per genus or species, early = the genera or species whose juveniles show early, late = those resembling another family or alike across species. trait: what to teach about them (sourced); obs: what Pierre observed (his own words, 2026-11-04). Mimicry is always a hypothesis: written as resembles or has been suggested. A juvenile photo is judged on the other criteria only (no juvenile cap) when its entry is A or its species is in early; every other juvenile keeps the cap: B and late for good (explanation cards later), C, ns and the rest provisionally (judging/FISH.md). The classes also say when a juvenile photo comes into its unit's draw (Pierre, 2026-11-17, Q391 a; core.js varKindOf, VAR_AT): A and early from the unit's first question, B and late at Advanced, the rest from Open Water to Advanced.

varAt: a family's own thresholds for its photo variants, beside juv, only where they differ from the defaults (core.js VAR_AT, Q391 a): {kind: [from, full]} on the bar of the unit asked, kind jE (an early-class juvenile), j (another juvenile), jL (a late-class juvenile) or ph (a sex or colour phase); e.g. {"ph": [0, 0]} brings a family's sexes from its first question. Read for the family's units and the genera and species hanging from it (model.js varAtOf).

dimorph: true when the presentation's phase lines say the sexes or colour phases look different (Parrotfish, Anthias): every photo shows one of those forms, so none is among the very easy photos of its first questions (judging/FISH.md).
species: one per line: PDF order, the slides, winks, then Dauin species of circle 3. id: stable, never reuse. name: the scientific name.
name: as written in the PDF, i.e. as EventMeasure names it (its fixed pick list may lag WoRMS): it stays the name shown (unless shown says otherwise) and
expected; the build adds the WoRMS accepted name beside it (now). A PDF species of a family in no circle, or not
confirmed in the Philippines, stays in fish.json out of the game (the future Fish ID Key holds every PDF species).
Confirmed = Research Grade on iNaturalist, or one of Pierre's own (ppericard) observations identified to the species,
even Needs ID (he names a species only when very sure); his only. The build computes it (presence()).
as: the name to look up when the written one does not resolve (hand fix of a typo or wrapped name).

shown: the name shown and expected instead of name, only by Pierre's decision (shownWhy: why, with his date); name keeps the PDF's spelling. The build looks it up in WoRMS as shown and adds now only when WoRMS accepts another name.

common: our common name, on a species of another source (dauin, wink, slides); the PDF species' name (as in the PDF, never corrected) is the instance's, in its layer. src: dauin or wink here; a species with no src is the PDF's (the layer gives it pdf), slides (the presentation alone) is the layer's.
sec, pdf, cs: the PDF's section, pages and cheatsheet rank (24 most sighted) of a PDF species: the instance's, in its layer.
sl: slide where the presentation names it (the instance's layer). check: a point for Pierre to check against EventMeasure (e.g. a likely slip).
photoTaxon: {inat, name, note, src, why}: the candidate photos come from this other iNaturalist taxon (tools/fetch_fish.py
photo_taxon), e.g. the Pacific form iNaturalist splits off; name, inat (presence, commonness, links) and the IMR name on
screen stay the species' own (Pierre, 2026-11-14, Q354 b). The admin says where its photos come from.

keys.cite: Allen, G., Steene, R., Humann, P. & DeLoach, N. (2015). Reef Fish Identification – Tropical Pacific, 2nd ed. New World Publications. ISBN 978-1-878348-60-9
keys.src: the book's index of its Twenty Identification Groups (group title, pages, the family labels under its drawings), transcribed 2026-11-04 from Pierre's screenshots (Drive, 01_ReefRecall/01_Ressources/Fish ID Groups - Indo Pacific)

groups.title: Small Ovals – Damselfishes
labels: anemonefishes (WoRMS files Amphiprion directly under Pomacentridae, so Pomacentridae carries them)

groups.title: Silvery
labels: grunters as Terapontidae; to check whether the book also means the javelin grunters (Pomadasys, Haemulidae)
WoRMS splits the halfbeaks into two families

groups.title: Slender Schoolers/Colorful
labels: WoRMS ranks the anthias as a family (Anthiadidae), formerly the subfamily Anthiadinae of Serranidae

groups.title: Heavy Bodies/Large Lips
labels: WoRMS files the soapfishes in Grammistidae and, for Diploprion, in Liopropomatidae (Diploprioninae)

groups.title: Swim with Pectoral Fins – Parrotfishes
labels: WoRMS: the subfamily Scarinae of Labridae

groups.title: Cryptic Crevice Dwellers
labels: the Indo-Pacific basslets as Liopropoma (Liopropomatidae); to check against the book's pages

groups.title: Small, Elongate Bottom Dwellers – Gobies
labels: WoRMS splits the gobies into Gobiidae and Oxudercidae

groups.title: Odd-Shaped Bottom Dwellers
labels: the seabed batfishes (Ogcocephalidae), not the Platax batfishes (Ephippidae, group 1)
the lefteye flounders; to check whether the book includes other flounder families

groups.title: Sharks & Rays
labels: Not a label of the book: added by Pierre's decision (2026-11-08, Q232), since in the Philippines, at Malapascua above all, this pelagic shark is seen on the reefs

juv.note: Dascyllus juveniles: black with white blotches, still clearly Dascyllus. Chromis and Pomacentrus: no juvenile source found.
Same disc shape; some Chaetodon juveniles add a rear dorsal black spot.
Pomacanthus juveniles: striking patterns unlike the adults (e.g. dark blue with electric blue and white rings). Centropyge: no juvenile source found.

juv.trait: very tall fins: greatly elongated dorsal and anal fins
juv.obs: They look much bigger than they are: very elongated dorsal and anal fins on a tiny body; as they grow, the body grows while the overall height hardly changes (Pierre, 2026-11-04)
juv.note: A resemblance to floating leaves or flatworms has been suggested, not established.
No source compares juvenile and adult colour; the horns are an adult feature.
Acanthurus pyroferus juveniles resemble Centropyge pygmy angelfish (another family). Naso, Zebrasoma, Ctenochaetus: no juvenile issue retained or no source.
Juveniles look similar to the adults (Siganus puellus); same body plan.
Small juveniles are striped, alike across species, and change pattern as they grow.

Coris gaimard juveniles: red to orange with black-edged white saddles; Novaculichthys juveniles are unmistakable (a resemblance to drifting seaweed has been suggested). Most Halichoeres and Thalassoma juveniles look alike across species.
Macolor juveniles: black and white pattern, very long pelvic fins. Lutjanus juveniles keep the snapper shape.
Not very different from adults but not specific at all: early juveniles share a few patterns of stripes and bands, told apart by close examination.
Scolopsis bilineata juveniles (black upper half with two yellow stripes) resemble the fangblenny Meiacanthus grammistes, another family. Other Scolopsis: no juvenile source found.
Plectropomus laevis juveniles resemble the Blacksaddle Toby Canthigaster valentini, a pufferfish. Cephalopholis juveniles differ in colour but keep the body plan.

juv.trait: head-down, wriggling (undulating) swimming with exaggerated fin movements; bold creamy blotches
juv.note: A resemblance to flatworms or nudibranchs has been suggested, not established.
No source for the IMR species; for a related one, females and juveniles share one colour description.
Same box shape at all sizes; Ostracion cubicus juveniles are bright yellow with black spots.
Barbels at all sizes.
Arothron stellatus juveniles: orange with dark stripes breaking into spots, unlike the adult but clearly a puffer. Other Arothron and Canthigaster: no juvenile source found.
Thin source: Aluterus scriptus juveniles drift head-down with floating vegetation, offshore.
Same feathery fin plan; juveniles mostly translucent.
